title: Safe and professional scripting
goal: Write scripts that stop on errors, clean up after themselves, never run twice at once, can run again safely, and give CI the right exit code.
setup: # P4: a server config the setup script must change only once
# P5: a CI step with problems, and a failing test runner

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# CI step: go into build/, run the tests, save the output in test.log,' '# and FAIL the job (exit code not 0) if the tests fail.' 'BUILD_DIR=build' 'cd $BULD_DIR' 'echo "building in $(pwd)"' './run-tests.sh | tee test.log' 'echo "tests finished"' > ci-step.sh
printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' 'name=$1' 'greeting="Hello"' 'if [ $name = "admin" ]; then greeting="Welcome back"; fi' 'echo "$greeting, $name"' > greet.sh

warmup.q: Which scenario check comes first when SSH fails: the key or the port?
warmup.a: The port (and the name before it). If `nc -zv host 22` fails, the key does not matter yet.

warmup.q: How do you create a unique temp file in a script?
What does `trap cleanup TERM INT` do?
warmup.a: It runs the function `cleanup` when the script gets SIGTERM or SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

warmup.q: What is wrong with `cmd && exit 1` as the last line of a script?
warmup.a: When `cmd` is false, the line is false, so the script exits with 1 even though nothing failed. Use `if cmd; then exit 1; fi; exit 0`.

problems.title: set -euo pipefail: what each part catches
problems.situation: Most production scripts start with `set -euo pipefail`. In an interview the user must explain each letter with an example. Each test runs in its own `bash -c`, so the main script keeps running.
task: Without options: run `false; echo "still running"`. Then the same with `set -e`.
Without options: `echo "Hello $NAEM"` (typo). Then with `set -u`.
Without options: `grep ERROR missing.log | wc -l; echo $?`. Then with `set -o pipefail`.
Predict each result before you run it. Write down which mistake each option catches.
hints: `-e`: exit when a command fails (with some exceptions, like inside `if`).
`-u`: an unset variable is an error, not an empty string.
`pipefail`: a pipeline fails if any command in it fails, not only the last one.
solution: bash -c 'set -e; false; echo "never printed"'; echo "with -e: stopped, exit code $?"
bash -c 'grep ERROR missing.log | wc -l; echo "without pipefail: exit code $?"'
bash -c 'set -o pipefail; grep ERROR missing.log | wc -l; echo "with pipefail: exit code $?"'

explanation.meaning: Stop the script at the first failing command. Not inside `if`, `while` tests, or before `&&`/`||`.
Using an unset variable is an error: `NAEM: unbound variable`, and the script stops with a non-zero code (127 here). Catches typos.
The pipeline's exit code is the last non-zero one. Without it, `wc -l` (success) hides grep's error.
All three in one line, near the top of the script.
With `-u`, use `${VAR:-}` for variables that may be unset on purpose.

problems.expected_output:
=== -e ===
without -e: still running
with -e: stopped, exit code 1
=== -u ===
without -u: Hello []
bash: line 1: NAEM: unbound variable
with -u: exit code 127
=== pipefail ===
grep: missing.log: No such file or directory
0
without pipefail: exit code 0
grep: missing.log: No such file or directory
0
with pipefail: exit code 2
mistakes: Thinking `set -e` catches everything: `if false; then ...`, `false || true`, and commands in `$( )` inside `local x=$(...)` do not stop the script.
Adding `set -u` to an old script and getting `$1: unbound variable` when no argument is given. Use `${1:-}` or check `$#` first.
problems.interview_say: `set -e` stops on errors, `set -u` makes unset variables an error, and `pipefail` makes a pipeline fail when any part fails. Together they turn silent bugs into clear failures.
problems.try_yourself: Run `bash -c 'set -e; if false; then echo yes; fi; echo "still here"'`. Why does `set -e` not stop here?

problems.title: trap EXIT + mktemp: always clean up
problems.situation: A build script downloads files into a temp folder. When it fails in the middle, old temp folders stay in `/tmp` and fill the disk. With `trap cleanup EXIT`, the cleanup runs on success, on error and on Ctrl+C.
task: Write `build-tmp.sh`: `set -euo pipefail`, create `WORK=$(mktemp -d)`, and `trap cleanup EXIT`.
In `cleanup`, remove `$WORK` and print the original exit code.
Make the script fail on purpose in the middle (`false`).
Run it, print the exit code, and check that the temp folder is gone.
hints: Save the exit code first in cleanup: `local rc=$?`.
Print the temp folder path to a file, so it can be checked after the script ended.
`[ -d "$path" ] || echo gone`
solution: echo "cleanup: removed the temp folder (exit code was $rc)"
[ -d "$(cat last-workdir.txt)" ] && echo "temp folder still there" || echo "temp folder is gone"

explanation.meaning: A new private temp folder (Day 13).
Run `cleanup` when the script exits for any reason: normal end, `set -e` stop, `exit N`, Ctrl+C.
The first line of the trap still sees the exit code that caused the exit.
Safe because `$WORK` always comes from mktemp; never `rm -rf` an unchecked variable.

problems.expected_output:
downloading into the temp folder
cleanup: removed the temp folder (exit code was 1)
script exit code: 1
temp folder is gone
mistakes: Putting cleanup only at the end of the script: with `set -e`, the end is never reached after an error.
`trap "rm -rf $WORK" EXIT` with double quotes before WORK is set: the trap gets an empty path. Use a function or single quotes.
problems.interview_say: I create temp files with `mktemp` and register `trap cleanup EXIT` right after, so cleanup runs whether the script succeeds, fails, or is interrupted.
problems.try_yourself: Add `trap 'echo "interrupted"; exit 130' INT` and press Ctrl+C during a `sleep 10` in the script.

problems.title: Lock file: never run twice at the same time
problems.situation: A backup runs from cron every 10 minutes. Sometimes one run takes 15 minutes, so two copies run at once and break each other's files. `flock` makes the second copy stop at once.
task: Write `job.sh` that opens a lock file with `exec 9> job.lock` and takes the lock with `flock -n 9`.
If the lock is taken, print `another run is active, exiting` and exit 1.
The job itself: print a message, `sleep 2`, print done.
Start one copy in the background, then a second one at once. Print the exit codes.
hints: `exec 9> FILE` opens FILE on file descriptor 9 for the whole script.
`flock -n 9` = try to lock fd 9, do not wait (`-n` = non-blocking).
The lock is released automatically when the script ends, even after a crash.
solution: echo "[$1] another run is active, exiting" >&2
bash job.sh second; echo "second run exit code: $?"
bash job.sh third; echo "third run exit code: $?"

explanation.meaning: Keep the lock file open as fd 9 until the script ends.
Take an exclusive lock; fail at once if another process has it.
The kernel releases the lock when the process ends. No stale lock files, unlike `touch lockfile`.
`flock -n /tmp/backup.lock /opt/backup.sh` in the crontab does the same without changing the script.

problems.expected_output:
[first] got the lock, working
[second] another run is active, exiting
second run exit code: 1
[first] done
first run exit code: 0
[third] got the lock, working
[third] done
third run exit code: 0
mistakes: Using `[ -f lock ] && exit; touch lock`: two runs can pass the test at the same moment, and a crash leaves the lock file forever.
Putting the lock file in a folder cleaned at reboot is fine; putting it in a shared NFS folder can be unreliable.
problems.interview_say: To stop overlapping runs I use `flock`: `exec 9>/var/lock/job.lock; flock -n 9 || exit 1`. The lock is released automatically when the process ends, so there are no stale locks.
problems.try_yourself: Use `flock -w 5 9` instead of `-n`. Now the second run waits up to 5 seconds. What happens?

problems.title: Idempotent setup: safe to run again
problems.situation: A server setup script is run again after every change. The first version added the same config line twice and failed on `mkdir` the second time. An idempotent script gives the same result no matter how many times it runs (like Ansible or Terraform).
task: Write `setup.sh` that: creates `data/logs` and `data/cache`, adds `log_dir=data/logs` to `app.conf` only if it is missing, and points `current` to `data`.
Print `created` / `already ok` for each step.
Run it twice. Show `app.conf` and `readlink current` at the end.
hints: `mkdir -p` never fails if the folder exists.
`grep -qxF 'line' file || echo 'line' >> file` adds a line only once.
`ln -sfn data current` can run many times.
solution: for d in data/logs data/cache; do
if [ -d "$d" ]; then step "$d" "already ok"; else mkdir -p "$d"; step "$d" "created"; fi
if grep -qxF "$LINE" app.conf; then step "app.conf: $LINE" "already ok"

explanation.meaning: Running it 1 time or 10 times gives the same end state.
Test the current state first; change only what is missing.
Quiet, whole line (`-x`), fixed text (`-F`): exact line exists?
Commands that are already idempotent.

problems.expected_output:
=== first run ===
data/logs                    created
data/cache                   created
app.conf: log_dir=data/logs  added
current -> data              ok
=== second run ===
data/logs                    already ok
data/cache                   already ok
app.conf: log_dir=data/logs  already ok
current -> data              ok
# todo-api settings
port=8080
log_dir=data/logs
mistakes: `echo 'line' >> file` without a check: every run adds another copy.
`useradd deploybot` in a setup script: the second run fails with `useradd: user 'deploybot' already exists`. Check with `id deploybot` first.
problems.interview_say: My setup scripts are idempotent: they check the current state and change only what is missing, using `mkdir -p`, `grep -q || echo >>`, and `ln -sfn`. That is the same idea as Ansible or Terraform.
problems.try_yourself: Change the config value to `log_dir=/var/log/todo` in the script. Should the script replace the old line? Use `sed -i` for that case.

problems.title: Find the bug: the CI step that is always green
problems.situation: In Jenkins, the job `ci-step.sh` is green even when tests fail. Looking closer: it does not even run in the right folder. The goal is in the comments: the job must fail if the tests fail.
task: Run `bash ci-step.sh; echo "CI sees exit code $?"`. Read the output.
Find 4 problems: a typo in a variable name, `cd` without a check, no `set -euo pipefail`, and `| tee` hiding the test result.
Fix them. Run again: the job must now fail with a clear exit code, and `build/test.log` must exist.
hints: `$BULD_DIR` is empty, so `cd` went to the home folder. `set -u` would catch it.
`cd "$BUILD_DIR" || exit 1` (or rely on `set -e`).
Without `pipefail`, the pipeline's exit code is the one of `tee`, which is 0.
solution: bash ci-step.sh; echo "CI sees exit code $?"
# CI step: go into build/, run the tests, save the output in test.log,
# and FAIL the job (exit code not 0) if the tests fail.
bash ci-step.sh; echo "CI sees exit code $?"

explanation.meaning: Bug 1: the variable was empty; `cd` with no argument goes to `$HOME`. `set -u` turns this into an error.
Bug 2: never continue in the wrong folder.
Bug 3: without it the script went on after every error.
Bug 4: `tee` succeeded, so the failing tests were hidden. With pipefail, exit code 1 reaches Jenkins.
With `set -e`, the script stops at the failed pipeline. Jenkins marks the build as failed.

problems.expected_output:
building in /home/wicky
ci-step.sh: line 7: ./run-tests.sh: No such file or directory
tests finished
CI sees exit code 0
--- fixed ---
building in /home/wicky/bash-practice/day22/build
running 12 tests
FAIL: test_create_todo
CI sees exit code 1
build/test.log
mistakes: Adding `|| true` to make a red build green. It hides real failures.
Checking only the console output in Jenkins. Jenkins decides red or green from the exit code alone.
problems.interview_say: CI tools only see exit codes. I start every CI script with `set -euo pipefail`, check `cd`, and remember that a pipe into `tee` hides failures unless `pipefail` is on.
problems.try_yourself: Run `shellcheck ci-step.sh` on the broken version (run Reset and setup again). Which warnings match the bugs you found?

problems.title: A logging function with timestamps and levels
problems.situation: When a nightly script fails, the team needs to know what happened and when. A small `log` function adds a timestamp and a level to every line, writes to a log file, and sends errors to stderr.
task: Write `log LEVEL message...`: print `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS LEVEL message`.
Append every line to `job.log` with `tee -a`. For `ERROR`, send the screen copy to stderr.
Add `info`, `warn` and `error` shortcuts. Use them, then show `job.log`.
hints: `printf '%s %-5s %s\n' "$(date '+%F %T')" "$level" "$*"`
For errors: `... | tee -a job.log >&2`.

explanation.meaning: Timestamp in ISO style; sortable and clear.
Level padded to 5 characters, so messages line up.
Errors go to the log file AND to stderr (Day 4).
Shows that the ERROR line went to stderr: it is missing on screen but present in the file.
Here only to hide the changing date and time in the printed log.

problems.expected_output:
2026-10-20 16:00:56 INFO  backup started
2026-10-20 16:00:56 WARN  disk is 85% full
--- job.log ---
INFO  backup started
WARN  disk is 85% full
ERROR upload to S3 failed
problems.output_note: The screen lines contain the current date and time, so they are different on every run.
mistakes: Logging secrets (tokens, passwords) by mistake with `info "using $TOKEN"`. Never log secret values (Day 26).
Using `echo $line` without quotes: the double spaces from `%-5s` disappear.
problems.interview_say: My scripts use a small `log` function with timestamp and level, write to a file with `tee -a`, and send errors to stderr, so both humans and log tools can read them.
problems.try_yourself: Add `logger -t todo-backup "$line"` to also send each line to the system log (journal or syslog).

problems.title: Debug with bash -x and ShellCheck
problems.situation: `greet.sh` prints `unary operator expected` when started without a name. The user traces it line by line with `bash -x`, then lets ShellCheck explain the bug and the fix.
task: Run `bash greet.sh` with no argument. Read the error.
Run `bash -x greet.sh`. Each `+` line is a command just before it runs. Find the broken test.
Run `shellcheck greet.sh`. Read the codes (SC2086 ...).
Fix the script and run it with no argument and with `admin`.
hints: In the trace, `[ = admin ]` shows that `$name` was empty.
ShellCheck says: double quote to prevent splitting.
`if [ "${name:-}" = admin ]` works with an empty name.

explanation.meaning: Print each command (with variables already replaced) before running it.
The empty `$name` disappeared, so `[` got only 2 words.
Turn tracing on and off for one part of a script.
One line per finding: file:line:column: level: message [code].
ShellCheck exits 1 when it finds problems; here we only want to read them.

problems.expected_output:
greet.sh: line 4: [: =: unary operator expected
Hello,
=== trace ===
+ name=
+ greeting=Hello
+ '[' = admin ']'
greet.sh: line 4: [: =: unary operator expected
+ echo 'Hello, '
Hello,
=== shellcheck ===
greet.sh:4:6: note: Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting. [SC2086]
=== fixed ===
Hello,
Welcome back, admin
problems.output_note: Ubuntu 22.04 has ShellCheck 0.8; the warning wording can be a little different.
mistakes: Leaving `set -x` on in a CI script: every command is printed, including secret values from variables.
Ignoring ShellCheck notes because the script works today. Most notes are bugs that wait for the right input (like a space in a name).
problems.interview_say: I debug scripts with `bash -x` to see each command with real values, and I run ShellCheck in CI to catch quoting bugs, unchecked `cd`, and unused variables before they reach production.
problems.try_yourself: Set `PS4='+ ${LINENO}: '` and run `bash -x greet.sh` again. What does the trace show now?

interview.a: `-e` exits on the first failed command, `-u` treats unset variables as errors, and `-o pipefail` makes a pipeline fail when any command in it fails.

interview.q: How do you make sure temp files are deleted even if the script fails?
interview.a: Create them with `mktemp` and add `trap cleanup EXIT` (or `trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT`). The trap runs on success, error and Ctrl+C.

interview.q: How do you stop a cron script from running twice at the same time?
interview.a: With `flock`: `exec 9>/var/lock/job.lock; flock -n 9 || exit 1`, or `flock -n /tmp/job.lock script.sh` in the crontab.
A script that can run many times with the same final result. It checks the current state before changing anything (`mkdir -p`, `grep -q || echo >>`, `ln -sfn`).

interview.q: How do you debug a bash script?
interview.a: Run it with `bash -x` (or `set -x` around a part) to trace commands, and run ShellCheck to find quoting and logic bugs.

recap.meaning: Stop on errors, unset vars, failed pipes
Only one run at a time

recap.cmd: grep -qxF line f || echo line >> f

recap.meaning: Never continue in the wrong folder
